Empirical scope: Table 1 covers 16 generators/platforms and 11 baselines under ProGAN-to-unseen-generator transfer. The reported average of 93.47% accuracy and 97.00% AP is substantially above FerretNet's 85.66%/90.43% and RIGID's 77.17%/82.38%.

The ablations provide some useful evidence: removing the discrepancy branch produces the largest decline, from 93.47% to 85.73% accuracy, while backbone, objective, semantic-branch, and residual-branch variants are also considered.

The manuscript is generally organized and visually readable. The method diagram, main comparison table, post-processing experiments, and theoretical appendix make the intended contribution easy to follow.
weaknesses: Soundness: Lemma 4.2 does not follow from Assumption 4.1. The assumption concerns tangent-versus-normal sensitivity of the encoder Jacobian, but the proof introduces an unassumed ordering of tangent and normal eigenvalues of the Hessian of G(x)=||J_f(x)||_F^2. Even that ordering does not ensure the claimed positive coefficient unless lambda_min_perp(N-m)>lambda_max_T m. More fundamentally, showing E[G(y+eta)]>G(y) around training anchors does not establish E_q[G]>E_p[G] without controlling the empirical-anchor average relative to the population. The claimed epsilon-independent c0 is also inconsistent with the proof's c0 proportional to epsilon_0^2.

The small-noise expansion claims an O(epsilon^4) remainder under only a C2 assumption; stronger smoothness and uniform derivative control appear necessary. The theorem is therefore not established as stated, undermining the paper's main explanatory claim that memorization makes the asymmetry universal.

The theory does not directly analyze RA-Det: it assumes an isotropic random probe, whereas RA-Det uses a label-supervised, image-conditioned U-Net perturbation. The appendix further asserts that training epochs monotonically decrease SIDE divergence without proof or measurement. The theorem predicts only a small-noise lower bound, not the reported large-noise decline or inverted-U behavior. Epoch correlations are weak for several encoders, including R-squared 0.033 for DINOv2, and no uncertainty estimates are reported.

The central causal interpretation remains confounded. Because the probing network is trained using real/fake supervision, it may first recognize appearance or dataset cues and then emit class-dependent perturbations, creating the measured asymmetry rather than revealing an intrinsic one. Semantic and residual branches can directly classify appearance. Missing controls include fixed/random versus learned probes, a probe-only detector, perturbations learned without labels, and tests of the raw asymmetry before detector training.

The evaluation does not rule out dataset-format or source bias. This is especially concerning because the model includes a median-residual branch and the paper itself discusses PNG/JPEG bias for DIRE. There is no controlled equalization of file format, resolution, compression history, or real-image source. Thus the very large cross-generator results do not yet support a universal behavioral cue.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits the perturbation bound epsilon, U-Net and classifier-head specifications, branch-fusion rule, loss weighting, balanced-batch construction, threshold-selection procedure, test-set sample counts, random seeds, and uncertainty across runs. The role and computation of the optional batch-level DCA quantity are unclear and inconsistent with the later description of the discrepancy branch. The claimed public code is identified only as 'GitHub' without a usable location in the manuscript.

The robustness study covers only mild JPEG compression and blur, with an incompletely specified evaluation pool and no confidence intervals. There are no evaluations under real-source/domain shifts, resizing or screenshots, stronger social-media processing, contemporary generators, mixed editing, adversarial evasion, or calibration. These omissions make 'universal' and deployment-oriented claims premature.

Presentation has several substantive inconsistencies: the abstract says 14 generators while the experiment contains 16; DCA is introduced but not clearly used or ablated; and the paper alternates between a covariance statistic and Euclidean distance when describing that branch. Baseline provenance and whether all methods were retrained under identical preprocessing are also unclear.

Limitations and ethics are not adequately treated. There is no dedicated discussion of false-positive harms to artists or photographers, demographic/content-domain bias, detector misuse, adaptive evasion, or the consequences of deploying a poorly calibrated binary detector. Reporting these limitations would not itself be a weakness, but their omission is material for this application.

strengths: The behavioral perspective is interesting: probing representation stability under controlled perturbations is a plausible complement to conventional semantic and forensic cues.

The evaluation covers 16 generator sources while training only on ProGAN. Table 1 reports strong average performance (93.47% ACC and 97.00% AP), including substantial gains on several unseen diffusion models.
The paper includes useful ablations of the backbone, loss, and detector branches. It also evaluates JPEG compression and Gaussian blur rather than reporting only clean-image performance.
The manuscript is generally organized and provides an appendix attempting to connect the empirical phenomenon to generator memorization.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is unsound as written. Assumption 4.1 concerns tangent/normal sensitivity of the encoder Jacobian, but the proof of Lemma 4.2 introduces a stronger, unstated curvature condition on the Hessian of G. Even that condition does not necessarily make c1 positive. Moreover, the proposed c0 is proportional to epsilon_0 squared and therefore cannot be a fixed positive lower bound for every epsilon_0 in (0, epsilon_bar], as the lemma claims.

Theorem 4.3 does not establish robustness asymmetry in general: its lower bound can be negative unless Delta exceeds B sqrt(M/2). It also analyzes small isotropic random noise, whereas RA-Det uses a learned, image-conditional perturbation. Consequently, the theory does not directly justify the proposed method or the claimed universality.

The empirical validation of the theory is unconvincing. Training epochs are asserted, rather than demonstrated, to be a monotonic proxy for SIDE divergence. The epoch correlations are weak (reported R-squared values approximately 0.337, 0.266, 0.440, and 0.033), especially for DINOv2. The theorem only covers the small-noise regime and does not predict the claimed large-noise decline or inverted-U behavior.

The experiments do not isolate the main claimed contribution. There is no comparison of learned DRP against random Gaussian noise, fixed perturbations, an unconditioned perturbation network, or no perturbation. Removing the discrepancy branch still obtains 85.73% ACC, indicating substantial reliance on ordinary semantic and residual appearance cues. Thus Table 1 cannot establish that robustness asymmetry, rather than the strong DINOv3 backbone and multi-branch ensemble, causes the gains.

Important method details are missing or inconsistent. The perturbation bound epsilon is never specified; pixel clipping and semantics preservation are not evaluated; the UNet, classification heads, and logit fusion are underspecified; and DCA requires distribution-level expectations but is presented as a per-sample feature, then conflated with the Euclidean distance d. These issues prevent reliable reproduction.

The evaluation reports no repeated runs, uncertainty, significance testing, test-set sample counts, or calibration/error analysis. Baselines also use different training sources and architectures, while RA-Det benefits from the much newer DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone. The paper lacks a controlled same-backbone baseline and tests only a legacy benchmark, making the broad 'universal' claim premature.

The claimed public code is only linked to generic 'GitHub' text with no repository address. The paper also provides no limitations or ethics discussion, despite deployment-relevant risks such as false accusations, demographic/domain bias, adaptive evasion, and degradation under post-processing—the reported robustness accuracy already falls below 80% at the strongest tested blur setting.

strengths: The behavior-based perspective is useful and reasonably original: detecting synthetic images through clean-to-perturbed feature drift offers a meaningful alternative to static semantic or forensic artifacts.

The headline empirical performance is strong. Under the stated ProGAN-to-unseen-generator protocol, RA-Det obtains 93.47% mean accuracy and 97.00% mean AP across 16 sources, substantially exceeding the strongest reported universal baseline.

The evaluation has good breadth, including GAN and diffusion generators, platform-generated images, JPEG and blur corruptions, two foundation backbones, and ablations of the loss and detector branches.

The ablations provide evidence that discrepancy features are important: removing that branch lowers accuracy from 93.47% to 85.73%. The residual and semantic branches also provide measurable complementary gains.

The motivation, architecture, and principal results are generally presented clearly, and the figures and tables are readable. The problem is significant because generator-agnostic detection remains practically important.
weaknesses: The theoretical centerpiece is not sound as written. Assumption 4.1 concerns tangent-versus-normal sensitivity of the encoder Jacobian, but the proof of Lemma 4.2 introduces an unassumed ordering of Hessian eigenvalues of the Jacobian energy G. Even that ordering does not imply the claimed positive coefficient without the stronger dimension-weighted condition lambda_perp(N-m) > lambda_T m.

The derivation of Lemma 4.2 also moves from a local expansion around training anchors to E_q[G]-E_p[G] > 0 without controlling the difference between the empirical anchor distribution and p. Moreover, its stated constant c0 is defined proportionally to epsilon_0 squared, contradicting the claim of one positive constant valid for every epsilon_0 approaching zero.

The theory analyzes small isotropic, input-independent noise, whereas RA-Det uses a learned, image-dependent UNet perturbation. Consequently, the theorem does not directly justify the proposed detector or its learned probing mechanism, and the manuscript overstates memorization as an explanation for universality.

The empirical validation does not repair this gap. Training epochs are asserted to be a monotonic proxy for SIDE divergence without measuring divergence or memorization, and the epoch correlations are weak for several encoders, including R-squared values of 0.266 and 0.033. The claimed non-monotonic large-noise behavior also does not follow from the stated small-noise lower bound.

Crucial reproducibility details are missing or inconsistent: the perturbation bound epsilon is not reported; the precise UNet, fusion rule, branch heads, and training schedule are underspecified; DCA is called optional and is not clearly used; and the text later describes the L2 distance as DCA. Code availability is asserted only through an unspecified GitHub link.

The learned probe is trained jointly with class supervision, yet there is no comparison against random Gaussian noise, fixed perturbations, or a matched clean-image classifier. Without these controls, it is unclear whether DRP exposes an intrinsic robustness asymmetry or simply functions as another high-capacity learned detection pathway. Perturbation visualizations and perceptual measurements are also absent.

Benchmark evidence is insufficient for the universal claim. Results are reported from a single training/test benchmark with many older generators, without independent datasets, recent generators, confidence intervals, repeated runs, or analysis of content and file-format confounds. Baseline training and evaluation consistency is also unclear, particularly because some diffusion baselines use ADM rather than ProGAN training.

The robustness study reports only aggregate curves for JPEG and blur, with no uncertainty or clear description of the aggregation set. These limited post-processing tests do not establish robustness to resizing, recapture, social-media pipelines, adversarial manipulation, or generator adaptation.

The limitations and ethics discussion is inadequate for a deployable detector. The paper does not examine demographic or domain-dependent false positives, calibration, consequences of falsely accusing authentic content, adaptive evasion, or dual-use concerns. Overall, the empirical idea is promising, but unsupported theoretical claims and missing controls currently prevent others from reliably validating the central interpretation.

strengths: Soundness/empirical: RA-Det obtains strong results on the main cross-generator benchmark: 93.47% mean accuracy and 97.00% mean AP across 16 generators, substantially exceeding the reported strongest universal baseline. Results remain similar when training on ProGAN, SDv1.4, or their mixture.

The ablations cover backbone choice, loss, probing strategy, margin, and detector branches. They indicate that the discrepancy branch is important and that learned probing outperforms Gaussian noise, blur, and resize perturbations.

Significance: Generalizable synthetic-image detection is important, and viewing detection through responses to controlled perturbations is potentially useful. Evaluation includes GAN, diffusion, autoregressive, and platform-generated images, plus JPEG and blur corruptions.

Originality: Robustness-based detection already exists, as acknowledged through RIGID, but learning a conditional probe and combining semantic, discrepancy, and residual evidence is a meaningful extension.

Presentation/ethics: The main method and experiments are generally organized clearly, computational costs are reported, and the impact statement appropriately warns against fully automated high-stakes use because of false positives and false negatives.
weaknesses: Soundness—theory: Lemma 4.2 is not established by Assumption 4.1. The assumption concerns directional sensitivity of the encoder Jacobian, whereas the proof introduces a stronger, unstated ordering of tangent and normal Hessian eigenvalues of G(x)=||J_f(x)||_F^2. This implication does not follow. The proof also concludes a uniform c0>0 for every epsilon_0 in (0,bar epsilon_0], but its constructed c0 is proportional to epsilon_0^2 and therefore approaches zero. Moreover, subtracting E_p[G] after averaging over finite training anchors requires an unprovided relationship between their empirical average and E_p[G].

Theorem 4.3 can give a negative, hence vacuous, lower bound unless Delta exceeds B sqrt(M/2). A lower bound that increases as M decreases does not establish that greater memorization causes a larger actual robustness gap. Thus the manuscript's central explanation that memorization makes the phenomenon universal is substantially overstated.

There is a mismatch between theory and method: the theorem analyzes small isotropic, label-independent noise, whereas RA-Det uses a supervised, input-conditioned UNet perturbation optimized to separate real and fake examples. The theoretical result therefore does not justify the learned probing mechanism.

The empirical validation of the theory is weak. Training epochs have very low reported linear-fit R-squared values for several encoders, including 0.033 for DINOv2, despite the text claiming a consistent trend. The AMS experiment omits sample counts, uncertainty, significance tests, and sufficient procedural details, and it validates a surrogate metric rather than the stated SIDE divergence.

The experiments do not isolate robustness asymmetry from ordinary detector capacity. There is no clean DINOv3 static-classifier baseline trained with the same data and recipe, no perturbation-only detector, and no full branch-by-branch combination study. BCE-only RA-Det already reaches 90.86% accuracy, so the gain attributable specifically to the claimed behavioral principle is unclear.

Baseline comparability is uncertain: RA-Det uses a recent, large DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone and 378M parameters, while many baselines are older or architecture-specific. The paper does not report controlled retraining with a common backbone, preprocessing, augmentation, data, and compute budget.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the claim of public code. Essential details are missing or ambiguous, including the perturbation bound epsilon, UNet channel/depth specification, conditioning implementation, branch-head and fusion architectures, loss weighting, optimizer settings beyond learning rate, threshold selection, random seeds, and exact test-set sizes. No variance or confidence intervals are reported.

The discrepancy description is internally inconsistent: Section 3 defines DCA as an optional covariance statistic, but the detector description calls the L2 distance d a 'DCA distance'; it remains unclear whether DCA is actually used. The covariance expectation and its inference-time computation are also unspecified.

The universality and practical-robustness claims are too broad. Testing finitely many benchmark generators and only JPEG/blur does not establish a universal deficiency, and there are no controls for real/fake source, resolution, encoding, or semantic biases even though the paper itself highlights such biases for DIRE. Adversarial adaptation, resizing/cropping, screenshots, recompression pipelines, and distribution-shifted real photographs are not evaluated.

Appendix Table 4 is misleadingly labeled: it lists recent and established generators, but its reported averages reproduce the main established-benchmark averages rather than transparently averaging all displayed columns. The abstract also says 14 generators while the main experiment reports 16. These inconsistencies weaken confidence in the reporting.

Presentation has several correctable issues, including malformed citations such as 'SIDE (?)', inconsistent notation and ambient dimensions, an unclear Figure 1 caption, and claims of an inverted-U or S-shaped theoretical prediction that are not actually derived by the small-noise lower bound.

Overall, the detector shows enough empirical promise to avoid a strong rejection, but the unsupported central theoretical claim, insufficient causal isolation of robustness asymmetry, comparison concerns, and missing reproducibility details currently outweigh the contribution. strengths: The behavioral detection perspective is interesting and potentially useful: probing representation stability under perturbations is a plausible complement to static semantic and forensic cues.

The empirical study is broad, covering 16 established generators, several recent generators, multiple detector families, two foundation backbones, post-processing robustness, training-source variations, component ablations, and computational cost.

Reported benchmark performance is strong: the main table gives 93.47% mean accuracy and 97.00% mean AP, substantially exceeding the listed universal baselines. Ablations also indicate that the discrepancy branch and learned probing contribute materially.

The impact statement appropriately warns against fully automated high-stakes use, acknowledges false positives/negatives and computational cost, and recommends human oversight and provenance mechanisms.
weaknesses: Soundness: the theoretical centerpiece is invalid as written. Assumption 4.1 concerns tangent-versus-normal Jacobian sensitivity, but the proof of Lemma 4.2 silently replaces it with inequalities on the Hessian of the Jacobian energy G; those inequalities do not follow from the assumption. The proof also uses an upper tangent-curvature bound as part of a lower bound without sufficient spectral assumptions.

Lemma 4.2 claims a fixed c0>0 uniformly for every epsilon_0 in (0, epsilon_bar], yet its derivation obtains c0 proportional to epsilon_0 squared, which tends to zero. It also moves from averages over training anchors to an expectation under the population p without a sampling or generalization argument. The O(epsilon^4) expansion appears to require stronger smoothness than the stated C2 assumption. Moreover, the theorem's bound can be negative and hence vacuous.

The theory analyzes small isotropic random probes, whereas RA-Det uses a supervised, image-conditioned UNet perturbation trained jointly with the detector. Thus, even a corrected theorem would not directly justify the proposed method or its claimed learned robustness signal.

The central interpretation is insufficiently identified. The supervised probing network can first infer generator-correlated appearance cues and then deliberately induce label-dependent feature shifts; this would create the measured asymmetry rather than reveal an intrinsic property of generated images. The manuscript lacks controls such as class-independent probes, held-out probe training, label-shuffled probes, or matched real/fake data that would distinguish these explanations.

The architecture mixes semantic, learned-discrepancy, and conventional residual-forensic branches. Removing the discrepancy branch still achieves 85.73% accuracy, while no comparison uses the same DINOv3 backbone and matched classifier capacity without behavioral probing. Consequently, the large headline gain cannot be cleanly attributed to robustness asymmetry.

The empirical validation of memorization does not measure the theorem's SIDE divergence. Epoch is explicitly not a validated monotonic proxy, while the AMS regressions provide only slopes and R-squared values, with no sample counts, uncertainty, significance tests, or controls for checkpoint quality. The claimed tangent-to-normal transition as noise grows is also not established by the isotropic-noise experiment.

Presentation and reporting contain material inconsistencies. Appendix Table 4 says its average covers all listed generators, but the reported averages exclude the seven recent generators; for Setting I, averaging all 23 accuracy entries gives about 89.57%, not 93.47%. The abstract refers to 14 models, the main experiment to 16, and the appendix lists 23. DCA is defined as an optional population/batch covariance statistic but is later conflated with the per-sample Euclidean distance and its actual use is unclear.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite extensive experiments: the crucial perturbation bound epsilon is not reported, and the UNet dimensions, fusion rule, branch architectures, loss weighting, evaluation-set sizes, threshold selection, random seeds, variance, and statistical uncertainty are missing. A claim that code is available does not repair the incomplete algorithmic specification in the manuscript.

Significance is limited by evaluation on a largely established benchmark with potentially confounded real/fake sources and no testing of adaptive attacks, resizing/cropping pipelines, screenshots, recompression chains, or genuinely in-the-wild prevalence. The strong numbers are promising, but they do not support the repeated claims of a universal detector or universal generative deficiency.

Originality is moderate rather than high: robustness-gap detection is already represented by the cited RIGID baseline. Learned conditional probing and multi-branch fusion are useful extensions, but the paper does not convincingly establish that they expose a new intrinsic phenomenon rather than provide a higher-capacity supervised detector.

strengths: The behavior-based perspective is interesting and potentially useful: replacing purely static appearance cues with learned perturbation-response features offers a meaningful extension of prior robustness-based detection, especially through the discrepancy branch and conditional probing module.

The empirical headline is strong. On the established 16-generator benchmark, RA-Det reports 93.47% average accuracy and 97.00% AP, substantially exceeding the strongest listed universal baseline, FerretNet, at 85.66%/90.43%. It also performs well when trained on either ProGAN or SDv1.4.

The evaluation is broad in several respects, covering GANs, diffusion models, autoregressive generators, two foundation encoders, alternative probing operators, branch ablations, post-processing robustness, and computational cost. The ablation in Table 3 usefully shows that the discrepancy branch and learned probe are consequential rather than decorative components.

The paper is generally well organized and the practical motivation is significant. If the claimed generalization survives stricter controls, the method could be valuable for synthetic-media detection.

The impact statement appropriately warns against autonomous high-stakes use, discusses false positives and false negatives, acknowledges additional computation and benchmark limitations, and recommends human oversight and provenance mechanisms. I see no unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central evidence for an inherent, universal robustness asymmetry is partly circular. The conditional UNet is trained with real/fake supervision specifically to create a similarity margin, so it could first recognize generator artifacts and then emit class-dependent perturbations that manufacture the observed gap. The paper does not test this alternative with generator-disjoint probe training, probe transfer without retraining, label-shuffled controls, or perturbations optimized independently of the detection labels. Figure 2 also does not clearly specify how its perturbations were obtained.

The theoretical justification has serious gaps. Assumption 4.1 concerns directional sensitivity of the encoder Jacobian, but the proof of Lemma 4.2 introduces an eigenvalue ordering for the Hessian of G(x)=||J_f(x)||_F^2 that does not follow from that assumption. It then moves from a local expansion around training anchors to E_q[G]-E_p[G]>0 without establishing that the anchor-average G equals or dominates E_p[G]. The claimed positivity additionally requires a dimension-weighted curvature condition stronger than the stated ordering. The covariance of q is also ε₀²I in Eq. 15 but becomes ε₀²I/N in the proof.

The theorem analyzes an isotropic random probe, whereas RA-Det uses an input-conditional learned perturbation. Consequently, even a corrected theorem would not directly explain the detector being evaluated. Moreover, the lower bound can be negative and hence vacuous, and increasing a lower bound as SIDE divergence decreases does not prove that the actual robustness gap increases. The claimed inverted-U noise dependence is not established by the small-ε theorem.

The empirical theory validation is weak. It does not measure SIDE divergence, uses only one DDPM training trajectory, omits checkpoint/sample counts and uncertainty, and reports regressions without confidence intervals or significance tests. Epoch is explicitly acknowledged as an unreliable memorization proxy, while the AMS regressions have only moderate R² values and insufficient procedural detail. Table 6 also contains an unresolved citation marker, 'SIDE (?)'.

Important reproducibility details are missing: the perturbation budget ε, complete UNet and cross-attention specification, branch-fusion rule, whether and how DCA is actually used, loss weighting, test threshold calibration, random seeds, dataset-specific sample counts, and exact robustness-test values. DCA is defined as a population covariance statistic but later appears to be conflated with the per-example Euclidean distance d. The claimed public code may eventually help, but the manuscript itself is not presently sufficient for reproduction.

The baseline comparison needs stronger controls. It is unclear which results were reimplemented versus copied, whether preprocessing and thresholds were matched, and whether baselines received comparable modern backbones, data, tuning, and compute. RA-Det has 378M parameters and 281G FLOPs, and no simple DINOv3 linear-probe baseline is reported, making it difficult to attribute gains specifically to robustness asymmetry rather than backbone strength, capacity, or ensemble cues.

Several reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence. Table 4 says its last column averages across generators, but for Setting I the displayed 93.47 is the average over only the 16 established generators; averaging all 23 displayed generators gives about 89.57. The abstract refers to 14 generators, the main table uses 16, and the appendix uses 23. The robustness plots lack exact tabulated results, and no confidence intervals or multi-seed variation are reported anywhere.

The claimed universality is broader than the evidence supports. Evaluation is benchmark-centric and does not cover hybrid or locally edited images, screenshots, social-media processing chains, adversarial adaptation, or systematic content/domain and demographic false-positive analysis. These omissions are particularly important for the high-stakes applications discussed by the paper. Overall, the idea and reported performance are promising, but the central causal claim and theory require substantial correction and better-controlled evidence before the contribution can be relied upon.
